cards.prompt: What is the difference between a performance problem and a scalability problem?

keyPoints.text: A system is scalable if adding resources increases performance proportionally
More performance can mean handling more units of work or larger units of work (e.g. growing datasets)
Performance problem: the system is slow even for a single user
Scalability problem: fast for one user, but slow under heavy load

cards.explanation:
Scalability is about how performance responds to added resources: a service scales if adding resources raises performance proportionally, whether that means serving more units of work or larger ones.

A quick diagnostic: if the system is already slow for a single user, it is a **performance** problem. If a single user sees it fast but it slows down under heavy load, it is a **scalability** problem.

cards.prompt: Define latency and throughput. What is the usual goal when trading them off?

keyPoints.text: Latency: the time it takes to perform an action or produce a result
Throughput: the number of actions or results per unit of time
Aim for maximal throughput while keeping latency acceptable

cards.explanation: Latency is about how long one action or result takes. Throughput is about how many of those actions or results you get per unit of time. The general guideline is to aim for maximal throughput while keeping latency acceptable.

cards.prompt: State the CAP theorem. Since networks are unreliable, what choice are you really making, and when would you pick each side?

keyPoints.text: Consistency: every read gets the most recent write or an error
Availability: every request gets a response, which may not be the latest data
Partition tolerance: the system keeps working despite network partitions
Networks are unreliable, so you must tolerate partitions; the real choice is consistency vs availability
CP: may time out waiting on a partitioned node; good when you need atomic reads and writes
AP: returns the most readily available (possibly stale) version; writes propagate after the partition heals; good when eventual consistency is acceptable

cards.explanation:
A distributed system can only support two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. Because networks aren't reliable, partition tolerance is required, so the real tradeoff is between **CP** (waiting on a partitioned node may end in a timeout error) and **AP** (respond with the most readily available data on any node, which may be stale; writes propagate once the partition is resolved).

Pick CP when the business needs atomic reads and writes. Pick AP when the business can allow eventual consistency or the system must keep working despite external errors.

cards.prompt: Compare weak, eventual, and strong consistency. Give an example system or use case for each.

keyPoints.text: Weak: after a write, reads may or may not see it (best effort)
Weak fits real-time uses like VoIP, video chat, and multiplayer games; memcached is an example
Eventual: reads will see the write eventually (typically milliseconds); replication is asynchronous
Eventual is used by DNS and email and suits highly available systems
Strong: reads see the write right away; replication is synchronous
Strong is used by file systems and RDBMSes and suits systems that need transactions

cards.explanation:
These patterns describe how copies of the same data are kept in sync.

- **Weak**: no promise. If you drop off a call for a few seconds, you don't hear what was said while you were gone.
- **Eventual**: asynchronous replication, so there's a short window where reads can be stale.
- **Strong**: synchronous replication, so a read after a write always reflects it.

cards.prompt: Explain active-passive vs active-active fail-over. What are the downsides of fail-over?

keyPoints.text: Active-passive: heartbeats between active and standby; if heartbeats stop, the passive takes over the active's IP
Active-passive downtime depends on hot vs cold standby; only the active serves traffic
Active-active: both servers handle traffic and share the load
Active-active needs DNS (public) or app logic (internal) to know about both servers
Downside: fail-over adds more hardware and complexity
Downside: possible data loss if the active fails before newly written data replicates to the passive

cards.explanation: Active-passive fail-over can also be called master-slave fail-over; active-active can also be called master-master fail-over.

cards.prompt: How is availability measured? How does overall availability change when two components are in sequence vs in parallel?

keyPoints.text: Availability is uptime as a percentage, described in 9s (99.99% = four 9s)
Three 9s allows about 8h 46m of downtime per year; four 9s about 52.5 minutes
In sequence: total = A(foo) × A(bar), so availability goes down
In parallel: total = 1 − (1 − A(foo)) × (1 − A(bar)), so availability goes up
Example: two 99.9% parts give 99.8% in sequence and 99.9999% in parallel

cards.explanation:
In sequence, the availabilities multiply, so every extra component below 100% lowers the total. In parallel, the service only fails when both components fail, so the total goes up.

The primer's table puts 99.9% at 8h 45min 57s of downtime per year and 99.99% at 52min 35.7s per year.

cards.prompt: What does DNS do, how does caching affect it, and what are the common record types?

keyPoints.text: Translates a domain name to an IP address
Hierarchical, with authoritative servers at the top
Results are cached by lower-level DNS servers, the OS, and the browser for a TTL, so they can go stale
Records: NS (name servers), MX (mail servers), A (name to IP), CNAME (name to another name)
Managed DNS can route by weighted round robin, latency, or geolocation
Downsides: lookup adds slight delay, management is complex, DNS can be a DDoS target

cards.explanation: Caching keeps DNS fast but means changes take time to propagate. Weighted round robin can steer traffic away from servers under maintenance, balance clusters of different sizes, or split traffic for A/B tests.

cards.prompt: What does a CDN buy you? Compare push and pull CDNs and say which kind of site suits each.

keyPoints.text: A CDN is a globally distributed network of proxy servers serving content close to users
Two wins: users get content from nearby data centers, and your servers skip requests the CDN handles
Push: you upload content to the CDN when it changes; minimizes traffic, maximizes storage
Push suits low-traffic sites or content that rarely changes
Pull: the CDN fetches from your server on the first request, then caches for a TTL; first request is slower
Pull minimizes CDN storage but can re-pull unchanged files after expiry; suits heavy-traffic sites
Downsides: cost, stale content before TTL expiry, and URLs must be rewritten to point at the CDN

cards.explanation: CDNs mostly serve static files (HTML/CSS/JS, images, video), though some support dynamic content. With pull CDNs, traffic spreads evenly because only recently requested content stays cached.

cards.prompt: What does a load balancer do, what extra benefits can it provide, and what are its downsides?

keyPoints.text: Distributes client requests across resources like app servers and databases, and returns responses to clients
Keeps requests away from unhealthy servers and prevents overloading
Helps eliminate a single point of failure
SSL termination: decrypts requests and encrypts responses so backends don't have to
Session persistence: routes a client to the same instance via cookies
Routing options include random, least loaded, session/cookies, layer 4, layer 7
Downsides: can bottleneck if under-resourced, adds complexity; a single LB is itself a SPOF, so run several (active-passive or active-active)

cards.explanation: Load balancers come as hardware (expensive) or software like HAProxy. SSL termination also means you don't need to install X.509 certificates on every server.

cards.prompt: Compare layer 4 and layer 7 load balancing. What does each look at, and what is the tradeoff?

keyPoints.text: Layer 4 looks at transport-layer info: source/destination IPs and ports, not packet contents
Layer 4 forwards packets to and from upstream servers using NAT
Layer 7 looks at the application layer: headers, message body, cookies
Layer 7 terminates traffic, reads the message, decides, then opens a connection to the chosen server
Layer 7 enables content routing, e.g. video traffic to video servers, billing to hardened servers
Layer 4 needs less time and compute than layer 7 at the cost of flexibility; the performance impact can be minimal on modern commodity hardware

cards.explanation: Layer 4 balancing decides from transport-layer header info and forwards packets with NAT. Layer 7 balancing reads the application-layer message itself, which lets it route by content, but it does more work: it terminates the traffic, reads the message, and opens a new connection to the chosen server.

cards.prompt: Why scale horizontally instead of vertically, and what does horizontal scaling require of your servers?

keyPoints.text: Vertical scaling = a bigger, more expensive single server; horizontal = more commodity machines
Horizontal is more cost efficient and gives higher availability
Servers must be stateless: no user data like sessions or profile pictures on the box
Keep sessions in a central store such as a database or persistent cache (Redis, Memcached)
Downstream caches and databases must handle more simultaneous connections

cards.explanation: Load balancers can help with horizontal scaling, which involves cloning servers and adds complexity. The primer also notes it is easier to hire people who know commodity hardware than specialized enterprise systems.

cards.prompt: What is a reverse proxy, what does it give you, and how is it different from a load balancer?

keyPoints.text: A web server that centralizes internal services behind a unified public interface and forwards requests to a server that can fulfill them
Security: hides backend details, can block IPs and limit connections per client
Scalability/flexibility: clients only see the proxy's IP, so backends can change freely
Can do SSL termination, compression, caching, and serve static content
A load balancer is useful when you have multiple servers doing the same job; a reverse proxy helps even with one server
NGINX and HAProxy can do both; downsides are complexity and a single proxy being a SPOF

cards.explanation: A load balancer is useful once you have several servers, usually ones serving the same function. A reverse proxy brings its benefits (security, flexibility, SSL termination, compression, caching, static content) even in front of a single web or application server. Some software, such as NGINX and HAProxy, supports both layer 7 reverse proxying and load balancing.

cards.prompt: What does ACID stand for in relational database transactions? Define each property.

keyPoints.text: Atomicity: each transaction is all or nothing
Consistency: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another
Isolation: concurrent transactions produce the same result as running them serially
Durability: once committed, a transaction stays committed

cards.explanation: ACID is a set of properties of transactions in a relational database, which is a collection of data items organized in tables.

cards.prompt: Compare master-slave and master-master replication. What downsides do all replication setups share?

keyPoints.text: Master-slave: the master handles reads and writes and replicates writes to slaves, which serve reads only
If the master dies, the system runs read-only until a slave is promoted or a new master is provisioned (promotion needs extra logic)
Master-master: both masters serve reads and writes and coordinate on writes; if either goes down, the system keeps serving reads and writes
Master-master needs an LB or app logic to choose where to write; most setups are loosely consistent or have higher write latency; conflict resolution matters more as write nodes and latency grow
Shared: data loss if the master fails before new writes replicate
Shared: replaying many writes can bog down read replicas, and more replicas means more replication lag
Shared: more hardware and complexity

cards.explanation: Slaves can also replicate to further slaves in a tree. One subtle point: on some systems, writes to the master can run on multiple threads in parallel, while read replicas apply writes sequentially on a single thread.

cards.prompt: Compare federation and sharding as ways to scale a relational database. What do they have in common, and what problems does each bring?

keyPoints.text: Federation (functional partitioning) splits databases by function, e.g. forums, users, products
Sharding splits one dataset across databases so each holds a subset, e.g. users by last-name initial or geography
Both: less read/write traffic per DB, less replication, more cache hits, and parallel writes with no single central master
Sharding also shrinks index size; if one shard fails others keep working
Both need app logic to pick the right database and make cross-database joins harder
Sharding risk: lopsided shards (e.g. power users); rebalancing is complex; consistent hashing reduces data moved
Federation doesn't help if the schema needs huge functions or tables

cards.explanation: Federation splits databases by function; sharding distributes one dataset so each database manages a subset of it. With federation, smaller databases fit more data in memory, which means more cache hits from better cache locality. With sharding, add some form of replication so a shard going down doesn't mean data loss.

cards.prompt: What is denormalization, why would you use it, and what does it cost?

keyPoints.text: Writes redundant copies of data into multiple tables to avoid expensive joins
Improves read performance at some cost to write performance
Reads often outnumber writes 100:1 or 1000:1, and complex joins can be disk-heavy
Helps avoid cross-datacenter joins once data is federated or sharded
Materialized views (PostgreSQL, Oracle) can manage the redundant copies
Costs: duplicated data, constraints to keep copies in sync add complexity, can be slower than normalized under heavy writes

cards.explanation: Denormalization trades some write performance for read performance. It fits systems where reads heavily outnumber writes and joins are expensive; under heavy write load, a denormalized database might perform worse than a normalized one.

cards.prompt: When do database indices help, how are they usually structured, and what do they cost?

keyPoints.text: Help columns you query with SELECT, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, JOIN
Usually a self-balancing B-tree: sorted data with logarithmic search, sequential access, inserts, and deletes
Indices take extra space (and memory)
Writes get slower because the index must also be updated
For large data loads it might be faster to disable indices, load the data, then rebuild them

cards.explanation: An index can keep data in memory, which speeds lookups on the columns you query but costs extra space and makes writes slower, since every write must also update the index.

cards.prompt: Name the four main kinds of NoSQL store. For each, give its core abstraction and what it is good for.

keyPoints.text: Key-value (hash table): ~O(1) reads/writes, simple or rapidly changing data like a cache layer; complexity moves to the app
Document (key-value with documents as values): query by document structure; flexible, for occasionally changing data (MongoDB, CouchDB)
Wide column (nested map of column families): high availability and scale for very large datasets (Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra)
Graph (nodes and relationships): complex, many-to-many relationships like social networks
Generally: data is denormalized, joins happen in app code, most lack full ACID and favor eventual consistency

cards.explanation: Some key-value and wide column stores keep keys in lexicographic order, which makes range scans efficient. Wide column values carry timestamps for versioning and conflict resolution. Graph databases are newer, so tooling can be thinner.

cards.prompt: What does BASE stand for, and how does it relate to CAP?

keyPoints.text: Basically available: the system guarantees availability
Soft state: state may change over time even without input
Eventual consistency: becomes consistent over time if no new input arrives
BASE chooses availability over consistency in CAP terms

cards.explanation: BASE is often used to describe the properties of NoSQL databases, most of which lack true ACID transactions and favor eventual consistency.

cards.prompt: What are the reasons to choose SQL vs NoSQL? Give a few kinds of data that suit NoSQL.

keyPoints.text: SQL: structured data, strict schema, relational data, complex joins, transactions
SQL: clear scaling patterns, mature ecosystem, fast index lookups
NoSQL: semi-structured data, flexible schema, non-relational data, no complex joins
NoSQL: many TB/PB of data, data-intensive workloads, very high IOPS
NoSQL-friendly data: clickstream/log ingest, leaderboards, temporary data like carts, hot tables, metadata/lookup tables

cards.explanation: The primer frames this as two lists of reasons: SQL for structured, relational data that needs joins and transactions; NoSQL for semi-structured or non-relational data, very large volumes, and very high IOPS.

cards.prompt: Why cache, and where can caches live in a system?

keyPoints.text: Speeds up page loads and reduces load on servers and databases
Absorbs uneven load and traffic spikes caused by popular items
Layers: client (OS/browser), CDN, web server/reverse proxy, database, application (Memcached, Redis)
App caches hold data in RAM; since RAM is limited, eviction like LRU keeps hot data
Avoid file-based caching; it makes cloning and auto-scaling harder

cards.explanation: Popular items skew how reads spread across database partitions, so a cache in front helps even out the load. Redis adds persistence and data structures like sorted sets and lists on top of plain key-value caching.

cards.prompt: Compare caching at the database query level with caching at the object level.

keyPoints.text: Query level: hash the query as the key and store the result
Query level is hard to expire: complex queries are hard to delete, and one changed cell can invalidate many cached queries
Object level: the app assembles data into objects and caches those
Object level: remove the object when its underlying data changes; enables async workers that build objects
Good things to cache: sessions, fully rendered pages, activity streams, user graph data

cards.explanation: Query-level caching suffers from expiration issues because one changed piece of data can affect many cached queries. Object-level caching treats data as objects, as your application code does, and removes an object from the cache when its underlying data changes.

sources.section: Caching at the database query level

cards.prompt: Walk through the cache-aside (lazy loading) pattern. What are its strengths and weaknesses?

keyPoints.text: The app talks to both cache and storage; the cache never talks to storage directly
Read flow: check cache, miss, load from DB, add to cache, return
Only requested data gets cached; later reads are fast
A miss costs three trips, which can add noticeable delay
Data can go stale if the DB is updated; mitigate with a TTL or write-through
A failed node is replaced by a new, empty node, which increases latency

cards.explanation: Memcached is typically used this way.

cards.prompt: Compare write-through, write-behind, and refresh-ahead caching. What can go wrong with each?

keyPoints.text: Write-through: app writes to cache, cache synchronously writes to the DB
Write-through: slow writes, but reads of just-written data are fast and the cache isn't stale
Write-through issues: new nodes stay empty until entries are updated (pair with cache-aside); much written data is never read (use TTL)
Write-behind: write to cache, then write to the DB asynchronously, improving write performance
Write-behind issues: data loss if the cache dies before flushing; more complex to build
Refresh-ahead: cache refreshes recently accessed entries before they expire; hurts performance if predictions are wrong

cards.explanation: The primer notes that users are generally more tolerant of latency when updating data than when reading it. Refresh-ahead can cut latency compared with read-through only if the cache accurately predicts which items will be needed.

cards.prompt: How do message queues and task queues help with slow operations? When is async the wrong choice?

keyPoints.text: Async workflows cut request times for expensive operations and allow precomputing work (e.g. periodic aggregation)
Flow: app publishes a job and tells the user its status; a worker processes it and signals completion
User isn't blocked; the client can make the task seem done (e.g. a tweet shows on your timeline before it reaches all followers)
Task queues run tasks and deliver results, and can support scheduling (e.g. Celery)
Async is a poor fit for cheap calculations and real-time workflows, where queues add delay and complexity

cards.explanation: Broker tradeoffs the primer calls out: Redis is simple but can lose messages; RabbitMQ needs the AMQP protocol and self-managed nodes; Amazon SQS is hosted but can be high-latency and may deliver a message twice.

cards.prompt: What problem does back pressure solve in a queue-based system, and how do clients react to it?

keyPoints.text: If a queue grows significantly it can become larger than memory, causing cache misses, disk reads, and slower performance
Back pressure caps the queue size to keep throughput and response times good for queued jobs
When full, clients get a server-busy / HTTP 503 response
Clients retry later, e.g. with exponential backoff

cards.explanation: Back pressure limits the queue size so jobs already in the queue keep a high throughput rate and good response times; clients that are turned away are told to try again later.

cards.prompt: For GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE: which are idempotent, and which are safe?

keyPoints.text: Idempotent means calling it many times gives the same outcome
GET: reads; idempotent and safe
PUT (create or replace) and DELETE: idempotent but not safe
POST (create / trigger processing) and PATCH (partial update): neither idempotent nor safe
HTTP is an application-layer request/response protocol over lower layers like TCP and UDP

cards.explanation: Idempotent means a verb can be called many times without different outcomes. The primer's table also marks GET as cacheable, PUT and DELETE as not cacheable, and POST/PATCH as cacheable only when the response includes freshness info.

cards.prompt: Compare TCP and UDP. When should you use each?

keyPoints.text: TCP is connection-oriented with a handshake; packets arrive in order and uncorrupted (sequence numbers, checksums, resends)
TCP has flow control and congestion control; these guarantees add delay
Use TCP when all data must arrive intact: web servers, databases, SMTP, FTP, SSH
UDP is connectionless; datagrams may arrive out of order or not at all; no congestion control; more efficient
Use UDP for lowest latency, when late data is worse than lost data: VoIP, video chat, streaming, games
UDP can broadcast to a subnet, which DHCP relies on

cards.explanation: Lots of open TCP connections cost memory, so connection pooling helps. UDP is also a fit when you want to implement your own error correction.

cards.prompt: Compare RPC and REST. What is each focused on, where is each typically used, and what are their downsides?

keyPoints.text: RPC runs a procedure in another address space as if it were a local call; focused on exposing behaviors
RPC is common for internal calls where performance matters (Protobuf, Thrift, Avro)
RPC downsides: tight coupling to the implementation, a new API per operation, harder debugging and caching
REST: clients act on server-managed resources; stateless and cacheable; focused on exposing data
REST uses URIs for resources, verbs for actions, status codes for errors; common for public APIs; statelessness helps horizontal scaling
REST downsides: awkward for non-hierarchical queries or actions outside the verbs, multiple round trips for nested data, payload bloat over time

cards.explanation: RPC calls are named after operations (e.g. `GET /someoperation?data=anId`), while REST calls name a resource and use a verb to act on it (e.g. `GET /someresources/anId`, `PUT /someresources/anId`).

cards.prompt: What are the four steps for approaching a system design interview question?

keyPoints.text: 1. Outline use cases, constraints, and assumptions: who uses it, how, how many users, data volume, requests/sec, read:write ratio
2. High-level design: sketch the main components and connections, and justify them
3. Design core components in detail (e.g. for a URL shortener: hashing, collisions, SQL vs NoSQL, schema, API)
4. Scale the design: find bottlenecks and address them (LB, horizontal scaling, caching, sharding), discussing tradeoffs
It's an open-ended conversation you are expected to lead

cards.explanation: You might be asked to do back-of-the-envelope estimates by hand; the primer's powers-of-two and latency-number tables help. Everything is a trade-off.

sources.section: How to approach a system design interview question

cards.prompt: Design Pastebin (or a URL shortener like Bit.ly): users paste text and get a short random link; anyone with the link can view it. Walk through requirements, estimates, high-level design, core components, and scaling.

keyPoints.text: Core: create paste → short link; view by link; optional expiration (default never)
Also: anonymous users, monthly page analytics, delete expired pastes, high availability
Assumptions: uneven traffic, fast reads, 10M writes and 100M reads per month (10:1 read:write)
~1.27 KB per paste → ~12.7 GB/month, ~450 GB and 360M links over 3 years
~4 writes/sec and ~40 reads/sec on average (about 2.5M seconds per month)
Client → web server (reverse proxy) → separate Write API and Read API → SQL DB for metadata + object store (e.g. S3) for contents
pastes table: shortlink (PK), expiration_length_in_minutes, created_at, paste_path; extra index on created_at
Short link: MD5 of IP + timestamp (or random data), Base62-encode, take first 7 chars (62^7 values); check DB for duplicates
Base62 over Base64 because + and / cause URL problems
Public REST API for create/read; RPC is an option internally
Analytics: MapReduce over web server logs since realtime isn't required; expiry: scan and delete/mark expired rows
Iterate: benchmark/load test, profile, address bottlenecks with tradeoffs, repeat
Memory cache for popular content and spikes; SQL read replicas for cache misses; single write master is fine at ~4 writes/sec
Analytics in a data warehouse (Redshift/BigQuery); consider NoSQL and further SQL scaling if needed

cards.explanation:
Bit.ly is the same problem except you store the original long URL instead of paste contents.

Don't jump straight to the final scaled design. Start simple, then explain which bottlenecks each added component (load balancer, CDN, replicas, cache) addresses and what it costs.
